Configuring the Widget Client

The widget client library gives applications a small, dependency-free way to construct and configure widgets for embedding in a dashboard. This guide walks through the basic configuration options, shows a minimal code example, and documents every option in a reference table at the end. Read through the whole guide before wiring the client into a production dashboard, since a few of the defaults are intentionally conservative and will need to be tuned for high-traffic deployments.

Start by constructing a client with a name. The constructor validates the name eagerly so that configuration mistakes surface immediately at startup rather than later when the widget is first rendered. Once the client exists, override any of the fields you need before calling Render. Fields left at their zero value fall back to the documented defaults, which are safe for local development but usually too small for production dashboards serving real traffic.

func NewWidget(name string) *Widget {
    return &Widget{
        Name:    name,
        Size:    10,
        Timeout: 5 * time.Second,
    }
}

func (w *Widget) Render(ctx context.Context) error {
    if w.Name == "" {
        return errors.New("widget: name required")
    }
    return renderTo(ctx, w)
}

Every configuration field is documented in the table below, along with its default value and a short description of what it controls. Options marked required must be set explicitly before calling Render, or the constructor returns an error describing exactly which field is missing so the mistake is easy to track down without reading the source.

OptionDefaultDescription
Name(required)Unique identifier shown in the dashboard header.
Size10Relative size of the widget grid cell, from 1 to 100.
Timeout5sMaximum time to wait for the widget's data source.
Retries3Number of times to retry a failed data fetch.

Once the table above is configured to match your deployment, call Render inside your dashboard's normal request handler. The widget client caches nothing internally, so callers that want caching should wrap Render with their own layer; this keeps the library small and keeps caching policy a decision made by the application rather than the library.
